title: What Gran Knew
part: PART THREE: WHAT THE MOUNTAIN KNEW

pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 18. Weather: fair. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. I have been a coward in ink for forty years.*

The rope tower smelled of dust and dried hemp. Mo climbed the ladder, his bare feet finding the rungs by memory, a habit as automatic as breathing. At the top, Gran sat at her desk, the Walk-Book open before her, but the pages were blank. She held her pen suspended in the air, staring at the wood grain of the table as if looking for a door.

Mo did not say hello. He did not ask how she was. Instead, he dropped his rope belt onto the table with a clatter that made her jump, the brass plumb-bob ticking against the wood.

"You know what she is doing," Mo said. "You know about the sea."

Gran’s hand trembled, and the pen hovered without moving. She did not look up.

"Who told you?" she asked. Her voice was thin, scraped raw like a chalkboard rubbed too hard by a lazy hand. She finally raised her eyes behind her huge spectacles. For the first time in Mo’s life, he did not see his sharp, brisk, ink-stained Gran. He saw a woman with deep lines around her mouth and eyes that looked very tired. She looked old. She looked small.
pages.image: Inside a wooden rope tower, a small boy in a green poncho stands before an old woman with a white braid and huge spectacles. She holds a pen in the air, staring at an open book, her face pale and serious, surrounded by coils of rope.

pages.text:
Gran set the pen down. She did not touch the book. Instead, she reached for her walking staff, the one with the brass bell that she carried everywhere. Her hands were steady now, but her movements were slow, as if she were handling something broken.

She unscrewed the top cap. A faint whiff of old paper drifted out. She slid a rolled page from the hollow shaft. It was brittle, yellowed, and cracked along the folds. It was not the ink of the current Walk-Book. The script was ancient, looping and faded.

"I found it forty years ago," Gran said. "In the back of a drawer in the Stepkeeper’s office. I didn’t read it right away. I put it back in the staff."

She unrolled the page on the desk. The words were clear, written by a hand that had been confident and calm. It described a meeting. It described a resting. It described an ending that was not an end.

At the bottom, in smaller letters, was a single note: *Do not fear it. It is a good ending.*
pages.image: An old woman’s hands unroll a brittle, yellowed paper scroll on a wooden desk next to a walking staff with a brass bell. The scene is quiet and intimate, lit by soft window light, focusing on the delicate, aged texture of the parchment.

pages.text:
"Why didn't you tell us?" Mo asked. He wanted to be angry, and he wanted to shout, but the words stuck in his throat, heavy and dry, like a spoon full of cold porridge.

Gran looked at the page, then at the blank book. "Because I am the Stepkeeper," she said. "I have kept the record of the Walk for forty years, and I am supposed to keep it going." She tapped the staff against the floor, and the brass bell gave a single, dull note. "If I told you, the Walk would end. I would be the one to write the last entry, and I did not want to be that person."

She picked up the staff, and her hands trembled just a little. "I was afraid of what the village would do," she admitted. "I was afraid of losing the life I know, so I thought if I didn't say it, it wouldn't be true." She looked at Mo, her expression tight and serious. "I thought the ink would stop the water. I thought I was protecting you."
pages.image: An old woman stands beside her walking staff in a dim wooden room, looking down with a pained expression. A small boy watches her, his face set in a tight, serious line. The atmosphere is heavy with unspoken words and quiet regret.

pages.text:
Mo did not reply. He walked to the corner of the tower, where the floorboards were worn smooth by centuries of feet. He sat down, crossing his legs, and he did nothing. He did not fidget. He did not check his plumb-bob. He just sat there, feeling the wood under his knees, feeling the hum of Tor far below, a low vibration in the air.

It was the hardest thing he had ever done.

Gran watched him. The silence stretched, filling the small space between them. It was not an empty silence. It was a full one, heavy with everything they had not said for days.

Finally, Mo spoke. His voice was quiet, but it cut through the air like a knife through cheese.

"You could have told me."

Gran closed her eyes. She opened them, and her face was soft, stripped of its usual briskness. "I should have," she said. Her voice was small, dry, and cracked. She reached out and placed her hand on the top of his head. It was the same gesture she had used when he was three and afraid of the dark.
pages.image: A small boy sits cross-legged on a wooden floor, looking up at an old woman who reaches out to touch his head gently. The room is dim, with warm shadows, capturing a moment of quiet, intimate connection and apology.

pages.text:
Gran lifted the brittle page from the staff. She did not tuck it away. She extended her arm, offering the paper to Mo.

"Keep it," she said. "You must keep it. And you must tell them. The whole truth, not the half-truths I have been hiding."

Mo took the page. It felt light, lighter than a cheese rind, yet it sat on his palms with a heaviness that made his shoulders ache. "They won't believe me," he said. "I am eleven. I am barefoot. I am no one."

"Exactly," Gran replied. She stood up, straightening her long white braid. "No one would believe an old woman who hid the end of the world for forty years. But they might listen to a boy who knows where they are going."

Mo stared at the faded ink, then looked up at Gran. Being listened to was far more frightening than being ignored. He had spent the entire week trying to be heard. He was not sure he could bear the noise of it.
pages.image: A small boy holds a rolled, yellowed paper page in his hands, looking down at it with a worried expression. An old woman stands behind him, looking resolute and tall, in a wooden room filled with ropes and light.
